text: Every breath you take travels down a tree. A tree that starts as one pipe in your neck, and ends in hundreds of millions of tiny air bags. Let's follow the air, from your nose all the way into your lungs.

Air enters through the nose or mouth. The nose warms, wets, and filters it. Then it passes the throat, called the pharynx, and the voice box, called the larynx. A small flap, the epiglottis, covers the airway when you swallow, so food goes down the right pipe.

Next is the trachea, or windpipe. It is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage, so it never collapses. Inside, sticky mucus traps dust and germs, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it back up to the throat.

In the chest, the trachea splits into two main bronchi, one for each lung. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more upright. That's why an inhaled object more often ends up in the right lung.
The two lungs are not twins. The right lung has three lobes. The left lung has only two, because it makes room for the heart, with a dip called the cardiac notch.
Inside each lung, the bronchi keep branching, smaller and smaller, into bronchioles. Like an upside down tree, the branches get thinner, until they end in clusters of tiny air sacs.

These air sacs are the alveoli. Each lung has hundreds of millions of them. Their walls are extremely thin, and wrapped in a net of capillaries. Spread out flat, they would cover roughly the size of a badminton court.
This is where the real work happens. Oxygen passes from the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes out of the blood, to be breathed away.

Each lung is wrapped in two thin layers called the pleura, with a little fluid in between. This lets the lungs glide smoothly as you breathe. And below the lungs sits a dome shaped muscle, the diaphragm.

So remember the path. Nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and finally the alveoli, where gas exchange happens. Right lung three lobes, left lung two. Next, we'll see how the diaphragm pulls air in, and how breathing really works.
